source_metadata.title: Improving Compliance with a Nurse-Driven Protocol for Unfractionated Heparin Infusions in Patients with Venous Thromboembolism
source_metadata.subtitle: A multidisciplinary initiative to optimize a complex process
source_metadata.institution: University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston

atoms.canonical_statement: The quality improvement initiative aimed to prevent UFH-related safety events by improving compliance with the institution’s nurse-driven VTE UFH infusion protocol.
The project used retrospective EHR-derived baseline and longitudinal compliance data to evaluate a multidisciplinary quality improvement initiative for a nurse-driven VTE UFH infusion protocol.

atoms.canonical_statement: The institutional VTE UFH protocol used an initial UFH bolus of 80 units/kg followed by a continuous infusion of 18 units/kg/hour.

Under the VTE UFH protocol, aPTT was measured at baseline, six hours after infusion initiation, and six hours after any infusion-rate change; after two therapeutic aPTTs, monitoring was reduced to daily.
At MD Anderson, the therapeutic aPTT range for VTE treatment with UFH was 60 to 100 seconds.

outcome.definition: aPTT 60 to 100 seconds for VTE treatment at the institution

atoms.canonical_statement: The baseline period (January 1 to July 17, 2019) included 200 UFH infusions; 56.5% were in men, mean age was 61 years (range 21–88), mean weight 84.9 kg (68.8–98.3), mean BMI 29.1 (23.7–32.6), and indications were VTE 83%, atrial fibrillation 11%, and other 6%.

population.label: Baseline UFH infusion orders, January 1 to July 17, 2019

atoms.canonical_statement: The planning/intervention period (July 18, 2019 to July 31, 2021) included 736 UFH infusions; 55.6% were in men, mean age was 63 years (range 17–92), mean weight 83.5 kg (67.3–95.7), mean BMI 28.9 (23.8–32.9), and indications were VTE 84%, atrial fibrillation 10%, and other 6%.

population.label: Planning/intervention-period UFH infusions, July 18, 2019 to July 31, 2021

atoms.canonical_statement: The postimplementation period (August 1, 2021 to December 31, 2022) included 473 UFH infusions; 54.5% were in men, mean age was 63 years (range 20–90), mean weight 83.1 kg (66.9–95.1), mean BMI 29.0 (23.7–32.7), and indications were VTE 85%, atrial fibrillation 9%, and other 6%.

population.label: Postimplementation UFH infusions, August 1, 2021 to December 31, 2022

atoms.canonical_statement: Institutional policy was updated to clarify the expected start window for continuous infusions and to require provider-directed off-protocol UFH changes to be documented by amending or replacing the protocol order.

exposures.details: Clarified continuous-infusion start timing and formal documentation of provider-directed off-protocol changes

atoms.canonical_statement: The VTE UFH order set was revised to instruct nurses to start the infusion after the baseline aPTT specimen was obtained without waiting for the result.

atoms.canonical_statement: A nursing communication order allowed nurses to discontinue a newly ordered baseline aPTT when an aPTT result was already available from the prior 48 hours.

atoms.canonical_statement: The EHR displayed recent aPTT results in the MAR and laboratory ordering screen and added a UFH infusion report consolidating infusion rate, boluses, weight, anticoagulant orders, aPTT results, laboratory tasks/orders, and hold orders.

atoms.canonical_statement: A dedicated UFH infusion communication order was created to specify dates and times for holding and resuming the infusion around procedures.

exposures.details: Specified dates and times to hold and resume continuous UFH infusions

atoms.canonical_statement: Pharmacy and nursing education created a comprehensive nursing module covering UFH infusion basics, protocol details, new EHR functions, and common errors identified in baseline review.

exposures.details: UFH basics, protocol details, new EHR functions, and common baseline errors

atoms.canonical_statement: Compliance data were reviewed every one to three months; each aPTT obtained during UFH infusion was assessed for timing and protocol adherence, duplicate or early unacted-on values were excluded from compliance effects, and values drawn less than five hours after initiation or dose change and acted on were classified as noncompliant.

source_anchor.paragraph: Methods — compliance data review and classification

atoms.canonical_statement: The quality improvement initiative was approved by the Institutional Quality Improvement Assessment Board.
The project set a goal to increase overall compliance by 10% from a baseline of 79.4% to 87.3% by December 2022.

Standards 2, 3, and 6—timely UFH initiation, timely aPTT collection, and timely protocol adjustment—were designated as the project’s key focus areas because baseline compliance was low and improvement opportunities were identified.
Standard 1 defined baseline aptt compliance as: Baseline aPTT obtained within 48 hours of UFH infusion start.

outcome.definition: Baseline aPTT obtained within 48 hours of UFH infusion start

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard 2 defined timely ufh initiation as: UFH infusion initiated within 60 minutes of the ordered start time.

outcome.definition: UFH infusion initiated within 60 minutes of the ordered start time

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard 3 defined timely aptt collection as: aPTT obtained within five to seven hours of drip initiation or dose change.

outcome.definition: aPTT obtained within five to seven hours of drip initiation or dose change

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard 4 defined aptt result process time as: aPTT specimen obtained, processed, and result recorded within two hours.

outcome.definition: aPTT specimen obtained, processed, and result recorded within two hours

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard 5 defined ufh protocol compliance for dose change as: UFH protocol followed when a dose change was indicated by the aPTT level.

concept.text: UFH protocol compliance for dose change

outcome.definition: UFH protocol followed when a dose change was indicated by the aPTT level

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard 6 defined timely protocol adjustment as: Infusion adjusted, when needed, within 30 minutes of the aPTT result.

outcome.definition: Infusion adjusted, when needed, within 30 minutes of the aPTT result

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard 7 defined transition to daily aptt monitoring as: aPTT laboratory draw changed to once daily after two consecutive therapeutic aPTT values.

outcome.definition: aPTT laboratory draw changed to once daily after two consecutive therapeutic aPTT values

atoms.canonical_statement: Standard 8 defined appropriate aptt draw during infusion as: Appropriate aPTT laboratory draw obtained while the patient was receiving the UFH infusion.

outcome.definition: Appropriate aPTT laboratory draw obtained while the patient was receiving the UFH infusion

atoms.canonical_statement: The postimplementation period had no recurrence of the identified never event in which the infusion was adjusted from the baseline aPTT instead of waiting six hours for a monitoring aPTT.
The postimplementation period had no recurrence of the identified never event in which the UFH infusion was started at a rate different from the provider-ordered rate.
The project did not achieve its prespecified 87.3% overall compliance target, although overall compliance improved from baseline.
aPTT ordering remained a manual process requiring nurses to calculate when the next laboratory test was due and enter the order.
Phlebotomy workflow could delay aPTT collection because many draws were performed by a phlebotomy team and scheduling required a nurse call to a dispatch number.
Timely infusion adjustment could still be delayed because nurses had to have the EHR open to see posted aPTT results and could be occupied with unstable patients.

source_anchor.paragraph: Limitations — aPTT result visibility and competing nursing workload

atoms.canonical_statement: The project used retrospective data collection, so some events could not be clarified with the bedside nurse after the fact.
The QI evaluation did not assess correctness of provider dosing by indication and weight or bleeding and thrombotic outcomes.

source_anchor.paragraph: Limitations — unmeasured dosing and clinical outcomes

atoms.canonical_statement: The project assumed that higher protocol compliance would be associated with a lower complication rate rather than directly testing that relationship.
The authors reported that very few UFH-related safety events and no serious safety events were reported after project completion.

source_anchor.paragraph: Conclusions — safety-event reporting after project completion

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the multidisciplinary initiative increased compliance with the nurse-driven VTE UFH protocol and decreased time to first therapeutic aPTT.
The authors disclosed no potential conflicts of interest, financial or otherwise.

extraction_limitations: This is an uncontrolled quality improvement report rather than a randomized or contemporaneously controlled comparative study.
The article reports compliance percentages in Table 2 without providing per-metric denominators or uncertainty estimates, so those details were not invented.
Bleeding, thrombotic outcomes, and correctness of provider dosing were not evaluated in the QI dataset and were not represented as measured outcomes.

The article reports post-project safety events qualitatively (very few; no serious events) without counts, so this was preserved as a qualitative result rather than converted to a quantitative result.
Figures 1 and 2 were reconciled against the reported Table 2 values and narrative trend statements; they did not add additional precise numeric results beyond those already atomized.
No external sources were used; background claims attributed to cited literature were not re-extracted as primary-study findings from this article.
